Event log channels
Which three classic Windows event logs exist alongside application-specific channels?
Application, Security and System
Kernel, Network and Storage
Audit, Debug and Trace
Login, Logout and Error
The classic logs are Application, Security and System; many more channels sit under Applications and Services Logs.
m
Event anatomy
Which fields identify what an event means?
Provider (source) and Event ID
Keywords and the task category only
The event's level and the computer name
The record number and the time created
Event IDs are defined per provider, so the pair identifies the event type.
m
Storage
In which format are Windows event logs stored on disk?
.evtx files
.csv files
.log text files
.json files
Event logs are stored as binary EVTX files, usually under System32\winevt\Logs.
d
Querying
Which PowerShell command efficiently retrieves failed logons from the Security log?
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625}
Get-EventLog -Failed -Security
Get-Content C:\Windows\Security.log | Select 4625
Find-Event -Id 4625 -All
FilterHashtable filters at the source, which is much faster than retrieving everything and filtering afterwards.
m
Logon events
What does Event ID 4625 record?
A failed logon attempt
A successful logon
A user logging off
A new user account
4624 is a successful logon, 4625 a failure, 4634 a logoff and 4720 a new account.
d
Logon types
Event 4624 shows Logon Type 3. What kind of logon is this?
A network logon, such as accessing a file share
An interactive logon at the physical keyboard
A Remote Desktop session
A scheduled task starting
Type 2 is interactive, 3 network, 4 batch, 5 service and 10 RemoteInteractive (RDP).
m
Account management
Which event shows that a user was added to a security-enabled local group?
4732 records a member added to a security-enabled local group, such as Administrators.
d
Process tracking
What does Event ID 4688 provide when process creation auditing is enabled?
A record of each new process, optionally with its command line
A record of each file read by any process
A list of processes that failed to start
The CPU usage of each running process
4688 logs process creation. Command-line logging must be enabled separately via policy.
d
Service installation
Why is System log Event ID 7045 useful in investigations?
It records a new service being installed, a common persistence method
It records the system clock being changed by an administrator
It records disk errors that may indicate hardware failure
It records Windows Update installing a new feature release
Attackers often create services for persistence or remote execution. 7045 shows the service name and path.
m
Audit policy
Why might a Security log contain no 4688 events at all?
Process creation auditing is not enabled by default
4688 events are written only to the System log
4688 events are deleted after each reboot
4688 events require a domain controller
Many audit categories are off by default. Advanced Audit Policy controls what is recorded.
d
Time
Why should event times be compared in UTC across machines?
Event logs store UTC; viewers show local time that differs by machine settings
Event logs store only the date, so time zones are irrelevant
UTC is required for Windows to write events at all
Local time is never recorded anywhere in Windows
Consistent time references are essential for building a timeline across systems.
m
Why centralise
What is a key reason to centralise Windows event logs?
Logs survive if a host is compromised or wiped
Centralised logs use less storage than local logs
Hosts cannot write logs without a central server
It removes the need for any audit policy
Central copies protect evidence and enable correlation across many systems.
d
WEF
How does Windows Event Forwarding deliver events?
Source computers send events to a collector using WinRM, based on subscriptions
The collector copies EVTX files over SMB from each host once per day
Domain controllers email events to administrators every hour
Events are uploaded to the cloud through the Windows Update service
WEF uses subscriptions (source- or collector-initiated) over WinRM; a SIEM can then read the collector.
m
Planning
When planning log collection, what should be decided first?
Which events answer the organisation's detection and investigation questions
Which colour scheme the SIEM dashboards should use
Which users may delete logs from their own machines
Which hosts may be excluded to save storage costs
Start from use cases; collecting everything without purpose is costly and noisy.
m
Workgroup versus domain
What is the main administrative difference between a workgroup and a domain?
A domain centralises accounts and policy on domain controllers
A workgroup centralises accounts on one elected computer
A domain can contain only one computer per user
A workgroup requires a separate licence for each computer
In a workgroup each computer has its own accounts; a domain uses Active Directory for central identity and policy.
d
AD building blocks
What is an organisational unit (OU) used for?
Grouping objects to delegate administration and link Group Policy
Holding the Kerberos keys for every user in the domain
Defining the security boundary between two separate forests
Replicating the directory between domain controllers
OUs organise objects for delegation and GPO linking. The forest is the security boundary.
d
Kerberos
Why does Kerberos depend on time synchronisation?
Tickets have timestamps and are rejected if clocks differ too much
Kerberos encrypts passwords using the current time as the key
Domain controllers shut down if a client's clock is wrong
Kerberos only works during configured business hours
Kerberos uses timestamps to prevent replay. The default tolerated skew is five minutes.
m
Cloud identity
What does Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) primarily provide?
Cloud identity and access management for apps and services
An on-premises file server for storing user documents
A replacement for the Windows kernel in the cloud
A local backup of every domain controller's disk
Entra ID is a cloud identity service; it is not simply Active Directory hosted in the cloud.
m
Group Policy purpose
What does Group Policy do in a domain?
Applies configuration and security settings to users and computers centrally
Encrypts all network traffic between domain members
Creates new user accounts automatically each morning
Backs up domain controllers to removable media
GPOs push settings such as password policy, audit policy and software restrictions.
d
GPO structure
Where are a GPO's files, such as scripts and templates, stored?
In SYSVOL on the domain controllers
In each user's NTUSER.DAT file
In the C:\Windows\Temp folder of each client
In the domain's DNS zone records
The GPO's container is in AD and its template files in SYSVOL, replicated between DCs.
m
Verifying policy
Which command shows which Group Policy objects applied to a computer and user?
gpresult /r
gpupdate /force
ipconfig /all
netstat -ano
gpresult reports the resultant set of policy; gpupdate refreshes policy.
d
GPO security
Why must write access to GPOs be tightly controlled?
A modified GPO can run code on every computer it applies to
GPOs store every user's password in plain text
GPO edits disable Kerberos for the domain
Changing a GPO deletes the OU it is linked to
GPO control is effectively control over the computers in scope, so it is a high-value target.
m
Servicing
What is Patch Tuesday?
Microsoft's regular monthly release of security updates
A day when Windows refuses to install any updates
The deadline for patching set by every regulator
A weekly reboot that Windows forces on servers
Microsoft releases security updates on the second Tuesday of each month.
d
Deployment rings
Why are updates deployed in rings (pilot, broad, critical)?
Problems surface on a small group before reaching everyone
Rings are needed because WSUS can update only ten machines at once
Rings ensure each update is installed exactly three times
Critical systems must always be patched first, before testing
Staged deployment balances speed and stability by catching compatibility issues early.
d
Drift
What is configuration drift?
Gradual divergence of systems from their approved baseline
Clock differences between domain controllers
Movement of users between OUs after promotions
Slow replication of SYSVOL between sites
Ad hoc changes accumulate over time. Regular comparison against a baseline detects and corrects drift.
m
Clearing logs
Which event in the System log shows that a log other than Security was cleared?
Clearing the Security log produces 1102; clearing other logs produces System event 104.
